sourceCurrency.scope: Injection-moulding-machine safety requirements and safe-use information within ISO scope; public abstract does not replace full standard or machine/site procedures.
General thermoplastic test-specimen injection-moulding practice; material specification or supplier guidance takes precedence.
Grade-specific example proving that recommended moisture, drying, melt/mould temperatures and residence limits are grade-scoped rather than universal.
Ultrason-family injection-moulding guidance including moisture/silver-streak and residence-time examples; family-specific, not universal.
Moulding and post-moulding shrinkage of thermoplastic test specimens, including directional shrinkage measurement.
Plastics moulded parts tolerances and acceptance conditions; current dimensional framework.
Thermoplastic moulding shrinkage test method; standard specimen behaviour must not be treated as an absolute production-part prediction.
Peer-reviewed review supporting multi-variable warpage/shrinkage mechanisms and process-parameter interactions; not a universal settings source.

claims.section: Safety is a system boundary
claims.claim: Injection-moulding machinery presents significant hazards that require engineered safeguards and safe-use controls.
claims.applicability: Injection-moulding machines within ISO 20430 scope.
claims.exclusions: Does not define a site-specific safe system of work or authorize intervention.
claims.basis: ISO 20430 explicitly covers significant hazards, hazardous situations/events, design/construction safety requirements and information for safe use.

claims.section: A stopped screen is not an isolation
claims.claim: A controller stop state must not be treated as proof that hazardous energy has been isolated or dissipated.
claims.applicability: Awareness principle for interventions around injection-moulding machinery.
claims.exclusions: Exact isolation and dissipation steps are machine- and site-specific.
claims.basis: The principle is safety-conservative, but verification requires applicable full-standard clauses plus machine-manufacturer and site isolation procedures; public abstract alone is insufficient.

claims.section: Guarding and interlocks are safety functions
claims.claim: Safeguards must not be bypassed as a generic production workaround.
claims.applicability: Machines using safety guards/interlocks.
claims.exclusions: Does not specify bypass modes permitted for authorized service under a validated procedure.
claims.basis: Consistent with the standard's machinery-safety scope, but the exact permitted modes/functions require the specific machine documentation and full applicable safety requirements.

claims.section: Moisture can affect appearance, processing and polymer integrity
claims.claim: Moisture effects are polymer-dependent and can include visible defects and, for hydrolysis-sensitive materials, polymer degradation during melt processing.
claims.applicability: Moisture-sensitive thermoplastics where supplier guidance identifies such mechanisms.
claims.exclusions: Not every polymer or grade has the same moisture sensitivity or failure mechanism.
claims.basis: BASF documents humidity as a cause of silver streaks for Ultrason; broader hydrolysis claims remain material-family/grade specific and require applicable supplier evidence.

claims.section: There is no universal drying recipe
claims.claim: Drying time, temperature and target moisture must not be treated as universal values across resins or grades.
claims.applicability: Thermoplastic materials requiring drying or moisture control.
claims.exclusions: A controlling grade-specific processing sheet may legitimately define values for that exact grade and stated conditions.
claims.basis: ASTM requires material-specific/supplier guidance to take precedence; BASF's current grade sheet provides explicit grade-specific moisture/drying values and dependencies.

claims.section: Keep the material dry after drying
claims.claim: Post-drying handling can matter because re-exposure may change the material moisture condition before moulding.
claims.applicability: Hygroscopic grades with supplier-defined moisture requirements.
claims.exclusions: Magnitude/rate of reabsorption is grade/environment dependent.
claims.basis: The current BASF sheet makes initial moisture/storage condition part of drying guidance; verification of specific reabsorption behaviour requires grade-specific handling documentation.

claims.section: Time at temperature matters
claims.claim: Residence time and melt temperature jointly contribute to thermal exposure and can affect product quality.
claims.applicability: Thermoplastics with supplier-defined thermal-processing limits.
claims.exclusions: No universal maximum residence time is asserted.
claims.basis: Both sources give material/grade-scoped residence guidance and relate excessive residence/temperature exposure to quality risks.

claims.section: Treat degradation as an evidence problem
claims.claim: Discolouration or black specks can be consistent with excessive thermal history but do not uniquely prove it.
claims.applicability: General troubleshooting.
claims.exclusions: Specific defect mechanisms require material/machine/mould evidence.
claims.basis: BASF links long residence/high melt temperature with discoloration and discusses black specks/residence time, but similar observations can have competing causes.

claims.section: What transfer means
claims.claim: Velocity-to-pressure transfer changes the process control objective from filling motion toward post-fill pressure control.
claims.applicability: Reciprocating-screw processes/controllers that implement a fill-to-pack/hold transition.
claims.exclusions: Controller terminology and available transfer criteria vary by machine.
claims.basis: ASTM supports standardized description/reporting of injection-moulding process stages but its public text is not sufficient to verify controller-specific transfer semantics.

claims.section: Why timing matters
claims.claim: An unsuitable transfer point can contribute to under-fill or excessive post-fill loading, but those outcomes are not uniquely diagnostic of transfer timing.
claims.applicability: General process diagnosis.
claims.exclusions: No universal transfer percentage, position or pressure is asserted.
claims.basis: Needs stronger primary/peer-reviewed process-control evidence and machine-controller documentation before publication-level verification.

claims.section: How to establish it
claims.claim: Transfer should be established from controlled experiments and actual process signals rather than copied as a universal percentage.
claims.applicability: Process development within safe material/machine/mould limits.
claims.exclusions: Exact procedure is not standardized here.
claims.basis: ASTM strongly supports material-specific conditions and consistent process reporting; a dedicated process-development source is still required for the proposed experimental method.

claims.section: What clamp force resists
claims.claim: Cavity/feed-system pressure acting over projected area creates mould-opening load that the clamping system must resist.
claims.applicability: Conventional injection moulding with separable mould halves.
claims.exclusions: Does not provide a sizing formula or safety factor.
claims.basis: Mechanically plausible and standard industry principle, but the public ISO safety abstract does not establish the detailed engineering relationship; an authoritative machine/process engineering source is required.

claims.section: Why a single formula is not enough
claims.claim: Actual clamp requirement depends on more than projected area alone and must remain within machine and mould ratings.
claims.applicability: Production machine/mould selection and setup.
claims.exclusions: No generic clamp-tonnage recipe is authorized.
claims.basis: Requires machine-manufacturer engineering documentation and/or a primary technical reference before verification.

claims.section: Mould protection is different
claims.claim: Mould-protection functions are machine-specific and are not substitutes for guarding, maintenance or correct tooling.
claims.applicability: Machines equipped with mould-protection functions.
claims.exclusions: Does not define setup parameters or prove a particular controller function.
claims.basis: Specific function meaning and setup must be verified from applicable machine-controller documentation.

claims.section: A heated feed system is part of the process
claims.claim: Hot-runner systems maintain molten material in part of the feed path and add heated flow-path/control elements relative to a fully cold runner.
claims.applicability: Hot-runner injection moulds.
claims.exclusions: Architecture varies across open-gate, valve-gate and supplier designs.
claims.basis: Current chapter anchors are insufficiently specific; add a current hot-runner manufacturer technical source before verification.

claims.section: Thermal history can differ by location
claims.claim: Local hot-runner thermal/residence conditions can affect melt condition and degradation risk.
claims.applicability: Material/hot-runner combinations where thermal exposure is relevant.
claims.exclusions: No temperature or residence threshold is asserted.
claims.basis: Requires hot-runner manufacturer evidence plus applicable material supplier guidance.

claims.section: Supplier instructions control
claims.claim: Start-up, shutdown, heater limits, valve-gate operation and maintenance must follow the installed hot-runner supplier's documentation.
claims.applicability: Installed hot-runner system.
claims.exclusions: Book cannot replace supplier procedures.
claims.basis: This is intentionally blocked until a representative current supplier source is registered; production application always requires the actual installed-system manual.

claims.section: Mechanism
claims.claim: Warpage is driven by non-uniform dimensional change and residual/orientation effects rather than one universal process variable.
claims.applicability: Injection-moulded thermoplastic parts generally; mechanisms vary by material and geometry.
claims.exclusions: Does not assert that every listed factor dominates every part.
claims.basis: Standards establish directional/test shrinkage concepts and the peer-reviewed review identifies multiple interacting process factors affecting shrinkage/warpage.

claims.section: Reinforced materials
claims.claim: Fibre orientation can make shrinkage and properties direction-dependent, influencing warpage in reinforced mouldings.
claims.applicability: Short-fibre-reinforced thermoplastic systems.
claims.exclusions: Magnitude and direction depend on grade, geometry, gate/flow pattern and process.
claims.basis: Peer-reviewed literature supports orientation/process interactions, but a dedicated fibre-orientation source is preferred before final verification.

claims.section: Do not use generic shrinkage tables as production predictions
claims.claim: Standard test-specimen shrinkage data must not be treated as an absolute prediction of a production part's final dimensions.
claims.applicability: Use of ISO/ASTM shrinkage data in production-part engineering.
claims.exclusions: Grade-specific data remain useful inputs when interpreted with geometry, process and mould conditions.
claims.basis: The standards distinguish standardized shrinkage measurement from the broader dimensional/tolerance behaviour of moulded parts.

summary.rule: Any hold or conflicting claim blocks chapter verification. Qualified claims require their stated scope to remain visible in publication wording.
